To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

single-path methods can be characterized by a single parameter (the generating path), that this path is entirely determined in a voluntary participation method, that there is a bijection between voluntary participation methods and distributions of rights, and that this characterization is not extendable to n >= 3 agents.

single-path methods are the only methods that are incentive-compatible and satisfy voluntary participation; that they are a bijection with the set of distributions of property rights over the production function of a single technology; that they do not generalize to more than two agents; and that they are characterized by their incentive properties in the 3-agent case.

single-path methods are the natural way to share technologies, that only one of them satisfies voluntary participation, and that this method is characterized by its incentives properties for n = 2 but not for n > 2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental question of the design of sharing mechanisms: how to share a single technology among a group of agents.
the design and characterization of mechanisms for sharing a production function among agents with private, decreasing returns production technologies.
the design of fair and efficient methods for sharing a production function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
single-path methods are not a natural way to pool private technologies.
the serial rule is the only single-path method that is both incentive compatible and individually rational.
, for n >= 2, single-path methods have a natural appeal but are too restrictive to be of much use in practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the set of single-path methods is not rich enough to capture all the desirable properties of a sharing mechanism.
single-path methods have a strong theoretical appeal and are the only methods that satisfy voluntary participation.
the serial rule is the only single path method satisfying voluntary participation, but there exist many other methods that do not.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the single-path approach can be extended to a larger class of production functions, and that the single-path method with the most incentives properties has a natural interpretation in terms of property rights.
, when agents have private technologies, single-path mechanisms are the only ones to be considered.
, in the context of sharing private technologies, the serial rule is a special case, and that there exist single-path methods that are better than it.
